scene.testo: You are floating in the dark, and you have been awake for ten seconds. There is no floor beneath you. There is no ceiling. You are strapped inside a sleeping bag, 250 miles above Earth, moving at 17,500 miles per hour. This is just Tuesday.

The alarm goes off, and it is the same on every orbit. Here is the first strange fact. While you slept for eight hours, the station circled Earth about five times. That means you saw five sunrises in one night. Welcome to the schedule of an astronaut.

So what do astronauts actually do all day? Most people picture a spacewalk, a rocket launch, a flag. The truth is quieter, stranger, and much busier. Stay with me, because one detail about the daily schedule explains almost everything about life up there.

Here is how the day begins. NASA astronauts on the International Space Station typically wake up around 6 AM. The station keeps Greenwich Mean Time, so the crew runs on one shared clock, no matter where each person came from.

There is no shower. There is no sink with running water. You wash with a damp towel and a small pouch of water. You brush your teeth, then you swallow the toothpaste or spit it into a towel. Water floats, so you have to be careful.

Then comes breakfast. Imagine a cereal bowl that will not sit still. Food is packed in pouches and sealed trays. Many meals are dehydrated, so you add water and wait. Drinks come in sealed bags with a straw. Spill something, and it floats away.

Here is a surprising detail. Astronauts have said that food tastes different in space. Fluids shift toward the head in weightlessness, which can leave you feeling stuffy, like a head cold. Many crews ask for spicy sauces, because bland food seems even blander.

By about 8 AM, the work begins. And here is the number that surprises people. Every day, the crew follows a detailed schedule, planned in blocks of minutes by teams on the ground. You do not wake up and decide what to do. Mission Control already decided.

A daily planning conference opens the day. Each morning, the crew talks with controllers in Houston, Texas. They review the schedule, flag problems, and ask questions. It sounds like a work meeting, except one side of the call is traveling 17,500 miles per hour.

Then comes the science. The station is a laboratory, and it has hosted thousands of experiments. Astronauts grow plants, study how flames burn, watch how fluids behave, and test how the human body changes. In weightlessness, nothing behaves the way it does on Earth.

Much of this work happens in gloveboxes and racks, with careful steps and checklists. One small mistake can ruin months of preparation. And some experiments are the astronauts themselves. They collect blood, measure muscles, and scan their eyes, to understand what space does to people.

Here is the hidden truth. A huge part of the day is not science at all. It is maintenance. The station is a machine that must stay alive. Air, water, power, and cooling all need constant care. Astronauts are scientists, but they are also plumbers and mechanics.

Think about the air. On Earth, you never think about it. On the station, systems remove carbon dioxide and make oxygen from water. If those machines fail, you cannot open a window. Crews check filters, replace parts, and fix things with tools they carry.

Then there is the toilet. Yes, it matters. A fan creates suction, because without gravity, nothing falls on its own. Urine is collected and recycled into drinking water. NASA has described it simply: yesterday's coffee becomes tomorrow's coffee. It is real, and it works.

At around noon, it is lunch. Crews often eat together, floating around a table, with food stuck to trays by Velcro and magnets. It is a small moment of normal life, and astronauts say these shared meals matter a great deal.

Now comes the part nobody expects. Every day, you must exercise. About two hours a day. Without gravity, bones and muscles weaken. Astronauts can lose bone density at a rate measured in percent per month, so the gym is not optional. It is medicine.

Picture this. You run on a treadmill, but you are strapped to it with a harness, or you would float away. You lift on a machine that uses vacuum cylinders instead of weights. And you pedal a bike bolted to the wall, upside down or sideways.

Why so much work? Because your body thinks it is on vacation. In weightlessness, your heart does less work, your muscles shrink, and your bones lose minerals. Two hours of exercise a day cuts the damage. It does not stop it completely.

Now, the spacewalk. It is rare, and it is huge. A spacewalk can last six or seven hours. Outside, the temperature swings from about minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit in shadow to about 250 degrees Fahrenheit in direct sunlight. That is minus 157 to plus 121 Celsius.

Before the walk, you spend hours getting ready. You breathe pure oxygen to clear nitrogen from your blood. You check every seal and every tool. The suit weighs hundreds of pounds on Earth, and it becomes your private spacecraft, with air, cooling, and a radio.

Then the hatch opens. Below your boots, Earth rolls by. The station moves so fast that you see a sunrise or a sunset about every 45 minutes. You work with your hands in thick gloves, and you always clip yourself to the station with tethers.

Let us compare. The station is about the size of a football field, including its solar arrays. It weighs roughly 925,000 pounds, which is about as much as 15 school buses. Inside, though, the living space is closer to a six-bedroom house.

That is the part that is hard to picture. Hundreds of feet of structure, and yet the crew lives in a small set of connected modules. You pass through hatches, floating from room to room. There is no up or down, only the direction you choose.

Mid-afternoon, there may be a call home. The crew can talk with family by video and phone, and some astronauts even take part in school events and live events with students. Everyone on the ground can see how normal and how strange the day looks.

Some days, the crew is also the cargo crew. When a supply ship arrives, you grab the station's robotic arm and catch it in space. Then you unpack food, equipment, and experiments. A single cargo ship can bring thousands of pounds of supplies.

By evening, there is time to rest, but even that is scheduled. Astronauts get some personal time. They read, watch movies, play music, or take photos of Earth. Many say the window, the cupola, is the best seat on the station.

Here is what they see. Lightning flashes inside storms. Cities glow at night. Auroras ripple in green. And the whole planet looks thin, with a faint blue line of atmosphere. Many astronauts describe this view as changing how they think about home.

Dinner follows, again in pouches and trays. Then you prepare for tomorrow. You check the schedule, answer messages, and write notes on your work. Then it is time to sleep. And sleeping in space is not like sleeping at home.

You crawl into your sleeping bag, which is attached to the wall. You can sleep in any direction. Your arms float up in front of you, so you tuck them in. There is no pillow pressing back, because nothing presses at all.

It is noisy, though. Fans and pumps run all day and night. Many astronauts use earplugs. And they often say sleep is harder than expected, because the sun rises every 90 minutes, and your body clock gets confused. Dark masks help.

So, add it up. Two hours of exercise. Hours of science. Hours of repairs. A spacewalk now and then. Meals, calls, cleaning, and paperwork. The truth is that astronauts spend their days working, with a tight schedule and little free time, and they love it.

Compare that to a day on Earth. You wake up, you walk across a floor, you shower, you eat breakfast at a table. Everything stays where you put it. In orbit, none of that is true. Every small action needs a plan, a tool, and a trick.

And then there is the cleaning. Every week, the crew spends time wiping surfaces, vacuuming, and checking for mold and dust. Dust does not fall in space. It floats, and it ends up in filters, so someone has to deal with it.

When the mission ends, the return is rough. Crews often come home in a Russian Soyuz capsule or a SpaceX Dragon capsule. Reentry heats the outside to thousands of degrees, and the landing is a hard thump on land or a splash at sea.

Then comes the strangest part. After months in orbit, gravity feels brutal. Astronauts can feel dizzy, heavy, and unsteady. Recovery crews often carry them out of the capsule in chairs, and they start rehab right away to rebuild muscle.

So what do astronauts actually do all day? They work, they fix, they exercise, they eat from pouches, and they float to sleep. But here is the most surprising detail. In their free time, many just look out the window. They say it never gets old.
